sections.h2: How should a Texas seller read the city and county guides?
sections.html:
Read the county guide for the place your house sits in first, because the appraisal district, tax office and clerk that touch your sale are all organized by county. Then use the city page for neighborhood facts, local permits and market context.

Texas covers 261,267.85 square miles of land, according to Census QuickFacts, and has 254 counties. Harris County has over 4 million residents and Loving County just over 100, so staffing, office hours and wait times differ a great deal even though the statutes are identical.

sections.h2: Who sets and collects property tax in Texas?
sections.html:
No state body taxes real estate here. Counties, cities, school districts and special districts each set a rate, and two separate offices handle the money side.

  • The appraisal district, run by a chief appraiser under a board, assigns value and handles exemptions.
  • An appraisal review board listens to owners who dispute a value.
  • The county tax assessor-collector commonly bills and collects for several units at once.

In counties with 75,000 or more people the assessor-collector holds a seat on the district board as an ex officio member. A seller often needs both offices: one for exemption status, the other for a payoff figure.

sections.h2: Which property tax dates matter most to a seller?
sections.html:
Five recurring dates shape most closings, as the Comptroller's deadline calendar prints them.

Texas property tax calendar highlights
DateWhat happens
January 1Values and exemption eligibility are set; the tax lien attaches
April 1 or soon afterAppraisal notices mailed to single-family homesteads
May 15Most protests due, or 30 days after notice delivery if later
October 1Tax bills mailed
February 1Unpaid taxes become delinquent

Owners may also split a bill, paying half by November 30 and the rest by June 30 of the following year.

sections.h2: What does a late Texas tax bill cost?
sections.html:
A late account picks up a six percent penalty and one percent interest the day it turns delinquent. After that the penalty gains a point each month until it reaches 12 percent in July, and interest has no ceiling.

A unit that hires a collection attorney can pile on as much as 20 percent. Residence homestead owners can request a payment plan, and the Comptroller notes that some collectors stretch it to 36 months. Ask the county tax office for a current payoff, since that is the number a title company wants.

sections.h2: Where does the county clerk fit into a sale?
sections.html:
The clerk acts as the county recorder for deeds, deeds of trust, releases, liens and foreclosure notices, and also takes probate filings and small estate affidavits. A deed is recorded where the land lies, not where the owner lives.

Recording needs a signed and acknowledged instrument, and fees are set by statute and published by each clerk. Call the office for its current schedule before closing day.

sections.h2: How does Texas foreclosure shape a quick sale?
sections.html:
Most home loans here carry a power of sale, so the lender can skip court. Reinstatement is open for 20 days after the default notice, and a notice of sale follows at least 21 days ahead of an auction held on a first Tuesday.

A homeowner with a posted date can sell first and pay the lender from the proceeds. After an auction, the lender has two years to sue for any shortfall. The State Law Library foreclosure guide walks through each stage, and a housing counselor can help before a date is set.

sections.h2: What do eviction and squatter rules mean for owners?
sections.html:
Landlords bring eviction suits in justice court after a written notice, normally three days. Trial comes soon: service at least four days ahead, a hearing within 10 to 21 days of filing, and a five-day window to appeal.

Property Code Chapter 24B gives owners a faster option against some squatters, a request to the sheriff or constable with no court case. It excludes family members and current or former tenants, and requires that the property was closed to the public when entered.

sections.h2: How do probate and inheritance affect a Texas house?
sections.html:
A will can go to probate up to four years after a death, generally in the decedent's home county. Smaller or simpler estates may use a muniment of title, a small estate affidavit or an affidavit of heirship.

Texas repealed its inheritance tax in 2015, so an heir mainly meets property tax and recording steps. Federal estate tax returns are required only above an IRS threshold that is $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026.

sections.h2: What paperwork should a Texas seller gather first?
sections.html:
Collect the documents that answer the questions a buyer, lender and title company will ask, so the closing date is not held up by a missing page.

  • The latest notice of appraised value from the appraisal district.
  • The current tax statement and a payoff figure from the county tax office.
  • The recorded deed showing how you took title.
  • Proof of any exemption on the property, such as homestead, over-65 or disabled veteran status.
  • Any lien release, court order or affidavit that a past estate or loan left behind.

If a document is missing, the county clerk can usually supply copies of anything recorded, and the appraisal district can confirm exemptions on file.

sections.h2: Which Texas guides fit which situation?
sections.html:
Match the guide to the problem you are solving, and expect to read more than one.

  • Behind on taxes or facing a bill you think is wrong: the property tax and protest material, plus your county page.
  • Inherited a house: probate, heirship and homestead pages, plus the county clerk guide.
  • Behind on a mortgage: the foreclosure material and the sale-before-auction option.
  • Landlord with a difficult occupant: the eviction and squatter pages.
  • Curious about value: the housing market page with FHFA and Census data.

Each guide names the official page it draws on, so you can check a rule or date at the source before you act on it.

sections.h2: Why does Texas exempt so many homeowners from part of the tax?
sections.html:
The state requires school districts to give every residence homestead a $140,000 exemption, adds $60,000 for owners who are 65 or older or disabled, and caps yearly increases in a homestead's appraised value at 10 percent. Disabled veterans get exemptions tied to a VA rating, up to a full exemption at 100 percent.

Those rules shape what a buyer inherits when a house changes hands. An exemption belongs to the owner who applied, so a buyer must file their own application, generally before May 1, and the seller's status does not simply transfer.

sections.h2: What happens if a Texas property goes to a tax sale?
sections.html:
Because a lien attaches each January 1, a court can order a delinquent property sold even after a change of owner. Sales are auctions run by a constable or the unit's agent, and the county clerk or tax office tells you where to find them.

Homestead, farm and mineral property can be redeemed for two years after the buyer's deed is filed, at a premium that rises from 25 to 50 percent in year two. Other property has about six months. Former owners have two years to claim leftover sale money.

faqs.q: How many counties does Texas have?
faqs.a: 254, from Harris County with over 4 million residents down to Loving County with just over 100, according to the Comptroller's county page.

faqs.q: Is there a state-level property tax in Texas?
faqs.a: No. Each local taxing unit sets its own rate, and the appraisal district values property as of January 1.

faqs.q: Which office do I call about my tax payoff?
faqs.a: The county tax assessor-collector, or the collector your taxing unit hires. The appraisal district handles value and exemptions, not payment.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed after selling a Texas house?
faqs.a: With the county clerk in the county where the land lies, on a signed and acknowledged instrument. Ask that clerk for the current fee schedule.
Not anymore. The inheritance tax was repealed effective September 1, 2015, and the IRS filing threshold for federal estate tax returns is $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026.
